source.title: Language Statistics and False Belief Reasoning: Evidence from 41 Open-Weight LMs
source.authors: Sean Trott; S. Taylor; Cameron R. Jones; James A. Michaelov; Pamela D. Rivière

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether model size predicts downstream task behavior, using false-belief-task accuracy and psychometric predictive power rather than held-out cross-entropy loss or the original scaling-law measurements.
record.gate_note: The study measures false-belief-task outcomes across model sizes and reports parameter-count associations. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, fit loss power laws, test extrapolation of loss, or identify compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.test_reason: Across 41 open-weight LMs, the paper regresses false-belief-task accuracy on log parameters and log training tokens. That bears on V6: downstream performance rising with scale, here on a new task. It fits no scaling-law runs and measures no loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested. T3 fits better than T2: this is an existing-model behavioural evaluation in a new setting, not a different method aimed at the original question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that larger LMs are more sensitive to knowledge states and better predict human behaviour, but none matches or explains away the human effect. Their headline point is about distributional statistics: these can account for the human knowledge-cue ("thinks") effect but not the knowledge-state effect. They limit claims to the sampled models.
record.recipe_differences: This is a downstream behavioral evaluation across existing model families, not a held-out-loss scaling-law sweep or compute-optimal allocation study.
record.method_sensitivity: For instruction-tuned models, question-format prompting produced slightly higher average accuracy than completion prompting: 62% versus 59.4% (Appendix B).

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models have higher psychometric predictive power for human false-belief responses: R² β=0.09, p<.001; ΔAIC β=−1.57, p=0.03.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LM-to-human behavioural alignment on psycholinguistic tasks increases with parameter count.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger models show a stronger knowledge-cue (non-factive verb) bias (β=−2.04, p=0.003).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sensitivity to lexical presupposition cues grows with model size.

record.code_released: The authors state that materials, data, and code will be published on GitHub after the anonymity period; no URL is stated.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study evaluates one behavioral task rather than held-out loss. The authors note that the model sample may not represent distributional learners generally and limit claims to the tested sample; accuracy was not perfectly monotonic with size.

untested.parts: Predictability from pretraining loss; fitted functional form or extrapolation of downstream scaling; tasks other than the false belief task.
All: no shape comparisons at fixed size.

missing.what: Log training-token count was not a significant predictor of accuracy (or of PPP) in the same regression.
Larger API models (Llama 3/3.1 70B, Qwen 2.5 72B, Mixtral 8x7B) reach 57.8%–73.4% accuracy, not exceeding the 13B model's 74.5%.
Only 14 of 41 models (34%) were significantly sensitive to knowledge state, and mean accuracy was 56.4%.

record.verdict_notes: This is not a scaling-law study. Scale is a regression covariate across heterogeneous model families, confounded with family, and no functional form is fitted. The V6 support is therefore weak and qualitative. Treat r2 and r3 as unlinked.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small runs predict much larger runs.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices on loss at fixed parameter count.
The study tests downstream false-belief-task accuracy and psychometric predictive power against parameter count, not pretraining loss, other downstream tasks, or predictability from loss.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices and training setup.

rows.subject: All 41 tested models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Regressed mean false-belief-task accuracy on log parameter count, log training-token count, and instruction-tuning status.
rows.measure: Association between parameter count and mean false-belief-task accuracy
rows.value: Log Number of Parameters: β = 0.08, SE = 0.02, p < .001; approximately 8% higher accuracy per order-of-magnitude increase in parameter count. Model R² = 0.44.
rows.note: The paper reports a positive parameter-count association, but says the relationship is not perfectly monotonic; the best-performing OLMo 2 13B model was about half the size of the largest models tested.
rows.check: State is right. The positive slope (β=0.08 per order of magnitude) explains only part of the variance (R²=0.44). The trend is not monotonic: OLMo 2 13B beat 32B models. Mean accuracy was 56.4%, and only 14/41 models were significantly sensitive. Subject size range is not stated in the row; it is roughly 14M–32B.

rows.subject: All 41 tested models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Regressed psychometric predictive power on log parameter count, log training-token count, and instruction-tuning status.

conditions.value: PPP: R² for predicting by-item human Log Odds from model Log Odds

rows.measure: Association between parameter count and psychometric predictive power (PPP)
rows.value: Log Parameter Count: β = 0.09, SE = 0.02, p < .001
rows.note: The study reports that larger models had higher PPP. The best-performing model on this measure had R² = 0.26.
rows.check: Psychometric predictive power is how well LM log odds predict human responses. That is alignment with human behaviour, not downstream task performance, so it does not measure what V6 names. Moved to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: All 41 tested models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Related parameter count to the change in AIC when LM Log Odds were added to a model predicting human responses.

conditions.value: PPP2: change in AIC after adding LM Log Odds

rows.measure: Association between parameter count and PPP2
rows.value: Log Parameter Count: β = −1.57, SE = 0.68, p = 0.03; larger models achieved a relatively larger reduction in AIC.
rows.note: Lower ΔAIC indicates greater predictive contribution relative to the other predictors, including Knowledge State.
rows.check: PPP2 (ΔAIC when adding LM log odds to a model of human responses) is a human-fit measure, not task performance. Moved to fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: Aggregate across 41 locally run models, completion prompting
relationships.reason: Log parameter count significantly and positively predicts false-belief accuracy, about +8% per order of magnitude (r1).
relationships.display_finding: Log model size positively predicted false-belief accuracy, with an estimated increase of about 8% per order of magnitude.

relationships.condition: Individual models and other scale axes
relationships.reason: Per the text, beyond r1's slope: the relation is not monotonic (13B best), and log training-token count is not significant. API models up to 70B reach at most 73.4%, below 13B's 74.5%. Most models are near chance (r1; text).
relationships.display_finding: Performance was non-monotonic, with 13B reaching 74.5% versus at most 73.4% for API models up to 70B, while most models remained near chance and log training-token count was nonsignificant.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
